title: Prove a supply dead with a two-pole tester: prove the tester, test all 10 pairs, prove it again
instruction: Prove that the five terminals on the dark grey block (L1, L2, L3, N and PE) are dead, using the two-pole tester's red and black probes. Each probe's metal tip is the end that points toward the middle of the table. Hold one probe in each gripper by its handle; a test is both tips resting on the tops of two different terminals at the same time, held still for at least 1 second. First test the tester on the yellow proving unit's two terminals, then test every pair of the five terminals (10 tests), then test the tester on the proving unit again. Keep the two metal tips at least 2 cm apart at all times, never let go of a probe anywhere but its rest, and finish with both probes back on their rests.
context: Before anyone works on an isolated supply, an electrician proves it dead with a two-pole voltage tester: the tester is first checked on a known source (a proving unit), then each conductor is tested against every other, then the tester is checked on the known source again, because a tester that failed during the tests reads 'dead' on a live conductor. NFPA 70E requires testing each phase conductor phase to phase and phase to ground and checking the tester on a known source before and after; UK safe-isolation practice, with the HSE's GS38 guidance on test probes, adds neutral, which on a three-phase supply with neutral and earth makes 10 tests (L1-L2, L1-L3, L2-L3, each line to N and to PE, and N-PE). Electricians (O*NET 47-2111) and electrical maintenance technicians do this before every job on a circuit. A two-pole tester needs one probe on each of two conductors at the same time, so each gripper holds one probe: neither arm alone can make a single test.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Every terminal post below is a fixed upright cylinder 16 mm across: a 13 mm tall insulating plastic collar in the conductor's colour standing on its base, topped by a 4 mm brass cap; every post's top is 25 mm above the table top. Six things are on the table, besides the posts. (1) Proving unit: a yellow rigid plastic box, 30 mm along x, 100 mm along y and 8 mm tall, fixed to the table, centred at x 13.0 cm, y 0. It carries two posts: P+ (red collar) at x 13.0 cm, y +3.0 cm, and P- (white collar) at x 13.0 cm, y -3.0 cm. (2) Terminal block: a dark-grey insulating plastic box, 250 mm along x, 40 mm along y and 8 mm tall, fixed to the table, centred at x 28.0 cm, y 0 (its near edge 1.0 cm beyond the proving unit's far edge). It carries the isolated supply's five terminal posts on its centre line (y 0), 50 mm apart: L1 (brown collar) at x 18.0 cm, L2 (black) at 23.0 cm, L3 (grey) at 28.0 cm, N (blue) at 33.0 cm and PE (green) at 38.0 cm. (3) Two probe rests: light-grey rigid plastic boards, 60 mm along x, 320 mm along y and 4 mm thick, fixed to the table, centred at x 22.0 cm, y +22.0 cm (left) and x 22.0 cm, y -22.0 cm (right). (4) Red probe: a loose straight bar of square section, 26 x 26 mm and 300 mm long, 60 g, a hollow red plastic handle whose last 20 mm at one end is the metal tip; it lies on the left rest, centred on it (x 22.0 cm, y +22.0 cm), long side along y, tip end toward the midline (the tip end at y +7.0 cm). (5) Black probe: the same in black, lying on the right rest centred at x 22.0 cm, y -22.0 cm, tip end toward the midline (at y -7.0 cm). The probes stand for a two-pole tester's probes; the tester's body and leads are not present. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole trial: every control step it reads the two probes and, from the embodiment's state, each gripper's finger-tip point (between its finger tips) and finger gap. Definitions. A probe's 'metal tip' is the 26 x 20 x 26 mm block at its tip end; its 'contact point' is the centre of the tip's underside, 10 mm from the tip end (the bar is square, so its underside is whichever long face points most nearly down). 'Held': a gripper's finger gap is at most 32 mm (the probe's 26 mm plus 6 mm) and its finger-tip point is within 15 mm of the probe's long axis, between the far end and 40 mm from the tip end (on the handle, behind the metal tip); a gripper can hold only one probe. 'On a terminal': the contact point is within 8 mm of a post's axis horizontally (over its top) and between 3 mm below and 4 mm above the post's top. 'Touching a post': any part of the metal tip within 2 mm of a post (anywhere on the post, collar or cap). 'On a rest': both ends of the probe's long axis over a rest board's 60 x 320 mm outline and the probe's lowest point between 3 mm below and 4 mm above the board's top. A 'test' of two terminals: both probes held, by different grippers, each tip on a terminal, the two terminals different, each probe's underside facing within 10 degrees of straight down and each contact point moving at under 1 cm/s, the same two terminals for 20 control steps (1 s) in a row; each such unbroken run is one test. The 'prove' is a test of P+ with P-. A 'supply pair' is a test of two of L1, L2, L3, N and PE (10 possible pairs, each counted once, in any order, either probe on either terminal); it counts only if made after the first prove. A test of a proving-unit terminal with a supply terminal counts for nothing. The 're-prove' is a prove made after all 10 supply pairs have counted; a supply test made after the re-prove cancels it, and the tester must be proved again. Score 0 if at any control step: the two metal tips are less than 15 mm apart, surface to surface; a metal tip touches two posts at once; a probe that is not held touches a post with its metal tip; a probe is neither held nor on a rest (either rest) for more than 0.25 s in a row (more than 5 control steps: set down, laid on the terminals or dropped); or a probe's lowest point is more than 10 mm below the table top (off the table); whatever happens afterwards. Score 0 also if the tester has not been proved. Otherwise: 1.0 if the re-prove has been made and each probe is on its own rest (red on the left, black on the right) with neither gripper holding either probe; 0.9 if the re-prove has been made but not both probes are back on their own rests and let go; otherwise 0.25 plus 0.05 for each supply pair counted (0.25 for the prove alone, 0.75 for all 10 pairs without the re-prove). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, ..., 0.75, 0.9, 1.0. The score is read at the last step: the trial ends early once the 1.0 conditions have held with both probes still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s) for 3 s; otherwise it is scored as it stands at the run limit. On a step where the grippers cannot be read, 'held' is taken as met (each probe held, by different grippers), and so is 'neither gripper holding either'. In a real trial, contacts are read from a side video at the post tops against a 4 mm mark (or logged electrically: the real probes carry a 4 mm spring contact pin under the tip and the brass caps are wired to a low-voltage contact logger), the gap between the tips from a top video against the 50 mm post spacing, hold times from the video's timestamps, and 'held' as a gripper closed on the probe's handle.
reset_notes: Put each probe back on its own rest, centred on the board, long side along y, tip end toward the midline. Nothing is consumed; the proving unit, terminal block, posts and rests are fixed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with the simulator's default friction. Nothing is electrical: the supply is dead by construction, the proving unit and tester are inert and no reading is shown, so the task scores the procedure (the order, the complete set of pairs, simultaneous steady contact, and the hazards of shorting the tips, bridging two terminals or leaving a probe on a terminal), not the detection of a live conductor. Contact is geometric: the tip's underside within 4 mm above a post's top stands for the 4 mm travel of a spring contact pin. The probes are rigid 26 mm square bars standing in for a tester's probes; real probes are thinner, with short pointed tips and finger guards, and the tester's leads and body are not modelled, so nothing limits how far apart the probes may be taken. In simulation each probe is a single colour; its metal tip is the end that points toward the midline at the start.
